title: Rosalind and the Parish
premise: True-crime podcaster Freya Villalobos is hired by a dying woman, Rosalind Parish, to prove that her husband's murder never happened — because the man buried under his name isn't him, and the real one is still out there. As Freya excavates a thirty-year-old alibi stitched together by an entire village, she realizes Rosalind isn't asking for truth but for absolution before someone silences her. The trail leads to Freya's own mentor, whose career was built on closing this very case, and to a second body no one ever counted. In the end, Freya must choose between broadcasting the story that will make her name and protecting the one person — Rosalind's granddaughter — who survived the original lie; she airs everything except the girl's identity, and lets the parish burn itself down.
about_author: Tamsin Ishikawa spent a decade as a rural correspondent covering cold cases that never made national news, and it shows in her patient, unglamorous attention to small-town complicity. She writes from a farmhouse in North Yorkshire, where she claims the best research material is simply listening to what neighbors don't say.

chapters.title: The Advance
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. A cash-stuffed envelope arrives with no return address and one instruction: prove Harold Parish was never murdered. Freya, between seasons and quietly broke, takes the case against her own rule about clients who hide. Emotional beat: professional pride masking a hunger to matter again.

chapters.title: Ashcombe Parish Records
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She travels to the village where Harold Parish vanished in 1994 and finds a death certificate with no body ever independently identified. The archivist is helpful — too helpful, steering her away from certain years. Beat: first unease beneath the postcard charm.

chapters.title: The Widow Who Isn't
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, present day. Frail and oxygen-tanked, Rosalind listens to a voicemail warning her to stop 'the podcast woman.' We learn she sent the money herself. Beat: guilt worn like a coat she can't take off.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Alibi
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Eleven witnesses placed Harold alive in Leeds the night of his disappearance — identical phrasing, down to the pub he supposedly drank in. Rehearsed testimony. Beat: the thrill of the hunt curdling into suspicion of everyone.

chapters.title: Grave 44
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She pulls the exhumation file: dental records matched, but the dentist who confirmed them died in 2001. A photograph of the skull doesn't match Harold's dental chart. Someone buried a stranger under his name. Beat: the case flips from fraud to double crime.

chapters.title: What Rosalind Remembers
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Freya finally meets Rosalind, who admits she paid for the investigation but denies knowing why Harold fled. Her hands shake when Freya mentions the exhumation. Beat: sympathy tangled with the certainty she's lying.

chapters.title: The Constable's Notebook
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The retired constable who 'closed' the case keeps meticulous notebooks — except three pages torn out, dated the week after the disappearance. He warns her off with genuine fear, not malice. Beat: dread; the cover-up had official blessing.

chapters.title: Merritt's Closed Cases
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Her old mentor, DCI Merritt — now a celebrated lecturer on cold-case methodology — built his reputation on the Parish conviction of a drifter later died in prison. Freya requests his files; he invites her to lunch instead. Beat: loyalty beginning to feel like a leash.

chapters.title: The Granddaughter
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. Rosalind's granddaughter Nell, a nurse in Ashcombe, recognizes Freya from the podcast and begs her to drop it — then slips her a key to Rosalind's attic. Beat: protective love at war with inherited silence.

chapters.title: Attic Light
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. In the attic: letters from Harold, postmarked years after his 'death,' and a child's drawing signed with two names — Nell's, and one smudged beyond reading. Beat: heartbreak; Harold abandoned them to keep someone safe.

chapters.title: Two Names on a Drawing
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. Nell confesses she had a twin brother, Peter, reported dead of fever in 1994. The records show no such child. Freya realizes the body in Grave 44 may be a boy, not a man. Beat: grief cracking open the family myth.

chapters.title: The Man in Leeds
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Following the letters, she finds Harold alive under another name — old, terrified, armed. He gives her one sentence before ordering her out: 'Ask Merritt what I carried for him.' Beat: vertigo; the victim is a witness.

chapters.title: Lunch with Merritt
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Merritt, urbane and generous, offers her a producing deal and gently suggests the Parish case ruined better investigators than her. She notices he still wears a watch Harold gave him in an old photo. Beat: betrayal anticipated but not yet proven.

chapters.title: What Harold Carried
chapters.summary: Harold's POV, 1994 flashback. A young PC Merritt falsified evidence in another case; Harold, the constable's informant, held the proof. When Merritt rose, Harold's silence was bought with a staged death and eleven rehearsed alibis. Beat: the machinery of survival revealed.

chapters.title: Peter
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, 1994 flashback. Her son Peter witnessed something through the hedge the night Harold 'died.' Days later the boy was gone; the village called it fever. Rosalind has spent thirty years paying for her silence with every breath. Beat: devastating maternal guilt.

chapters.title: The Second Grave
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Ground-penetrating radar on the old vicarage land — now Merritt's holiday cottage — shows a small grave. She records everything, then realizes she's been followed since Ashcombe. Beat: terror; the truth has a price tag and she's being measured for it.

chapters.title: Burn Notice
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Her flat is searched, her cloud backups wiped, her editor pressured to kill the series. Merritt calls: warm, reasonable, offering her the future she always wanted if she walks away. Beat: temptation at its most seductive.

chapters.title: Oxygen
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Someone cuts Rosalind's power during a storm; she survives on a backup tank while writing a full confession addressed to Nell. Beat: quiet courage; the dying woman chooses truth over safety at last.

chapters.title: Exhumation Order
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Using the constable's torn pages — which Nell stole back from his shed — Freya forces a fresh forensic review of Grave 44. The remains are a child aged nine. Warrant issued for the vicarage plot. Beat: triumph shadowed by countdown.

chapters.title: The Vicarage
chapters.summary: Climax, Freya's POV. At night, before police arrive, Merritt confronts her at the cottage with Harold as reluctant witness. Rosalind arrives, tank in hand, and plays her recorded confession aloud. Merritt breaks; Harold's testimony seals him. Beat: confrontation where truth outlasts violence.

chapters.title: Names Restored
chapters.summary: Falling action, multiple POVs. Merritt is charged; Peter's remains are named and buried beside his mother's plot; Harold, legally dead, chooses to stay dead rather than face prosecution, sending Nell his letters instead. Beat: justice imperfect but real.

chapters.title: Season Finale
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She airs the series — every name but Nell's, every crime but the family's survival choices. Downloads explode; Merritt's legacy collapses. Visiting Rosalind's grave with Nell, Freya finally understands some cases close people, not files. Beat: bittersweet resolution; truth kept, mercy chosen.
